systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : Eunews
Rubrique : Sanctions et export
Date du flux : 18/11/2026
Auteur : Iolanda Cuomo
Titre d'origine : The European Commission establishes the EU Sanctions Office

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (Eunews) :
Brussels – It will cover the entire “life cycle of sanctions.” From their definition through to implementation, including awareness-raising activities, measures to combat circumvention and dialogue with third countries. Today (18 November), the European Commission established the EU Sanctions Office, to bring together expertise from the Berlaymont Building and work on all aspects of restrictive measures. The new approach aims to ensure the coordination of EU sanctions vis-à-vis Member States and third countries and covers all sanction regimes. These include Russia and Belarus, as well as Iran, North Korea, Syria, organised crime and hybrid threats. According to a press release, the Office will provide support to Member States through faster guidance “on compliance, data sharing, and economic and technical analysis, with a view to ensuring the harmonised implementation and enforcement of sanctions within the Union.” The European Commissioner for Financial Services and the Savings and Investment Union, Maria Luís Albuquerque, welcomed the establishment of the Office, announcing that “the Office will strengthen coordination within the Commission, bringing together expertise from different policy areas to ensure a more coherent approach to sanctions, wherever and whenever the need arises.”
For Brussels, the role of sanctions has been redefined by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the EU’s subsequent response. Specifically, sanctions have become “a foreign policy tool and a key means of addressing major international challenges.” Since the start of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has adopted 21 rounds of sanctions; however, for the measures “to be effective, they must be fully implemented, rigorously enforced and protected against any attempts to circumvent them,” stated the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
The new unit will be established within the General Secretariat at the Berlaymont Building and will operate under the political responsibility of Albuquerque. A central aspect of its work will be “to support the EU Sanctions Envoy, a key figure in the Union’s efforts to prevent the circumvention of restrictive measures and to cooperate with partner countries.” This role involves liaising with third countries to reduce the risk of EU sanctions being circumvented, for example through alternative trade routes, financial channels, or supply chains. For this role, the European Commission today appointed the Swedish diplomat, Lars Danielsson, who will take up the post on 6 February 2027, following the end of the current Envoy’s term of office, David O’Sullivan. In the past, Danielsson held senior positions in the Swedish Prime Minister’s Office, including that of State Secretary for International and EU Affairs, while from 2016 to 2023, he also served as Sweden’s Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the EU. All the changes announced today will come into effect on 16 January 2027.
European sources who have worked on the initiative have explained that, since “Russia is one of the countries most heavily affected by sanctions in the world, and the sanctions regime against Iran (which has been fully reinstated) is also one of the most extensive, it was necessary to develop a completely new working system to prepare, define, monitor, and implement the packages.” An EU official pointed out that in the current geopolitical landscape, “for sanctions to be effective, a strategic approach is first and foremost required which, by drawing on intelligence, enables an adversary’s weaknesses to be identified”. Secondly, “analytical capacity is required to understand supply chains and the various economic sectors.” Thirdly, “access to intelligence and consistency across different policies are necessary.” Finally, “the capacity to manage the implementation and enforcement of the measures is required.” He noted that “at present, this task is entrusted to individual Member States, with highly inconsistent results that create conditions of inequality, gaps and loopholes in the system”. The official pointed out that “at present, activities relating to sanctions are divided between the Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and the Capital Markets Union (DG FISMA), the Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security (DG TRADE), the Office of the Special Envoy and the General Secretariat.” The optimal solution “is to bring all these functions together within a single office,” which will become “solely responsible for drafting new measures,” following the College of Commissioners’ decision to “establish this office as a body with a high degree of autonomy,” he concluded.
English version by the Translation Service of Withub

SOURCE 2 (INSIGHT EU MONITORING) :
Brussels, 18 November 2026
On Wednesday, the Commission has created the EU Sanctions Office to bring together the Commission’s expertise on the entire sanctions lifecycle, from policy design to implementation, enforcement, and anti-circumvention, including outreach to and engagement with third countries. This approach will ensure the role of sanctions coordination for the EU vis-à-vis Member States and third countries and is relevant for all sanctions regimes, in particular Russia and Belarus but also Iran, North Korea, Syria, and hybrid and organised crime. It will support Member States with faster compliance guidance, data sharing, and economic and technical analysis to ensure harmonised implementation and enforcement of our sanctions.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the EU’s response reshaped sanctions as a foreign policy tool and as a key instrument of the EU’s response to major international challenges. Since the start of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has adopted 21 packages of sanctions. As the demands on designing and implementing sanctions evolve, strengthening the Commission’s capacities and structures is essential.
The scale and complexity of these measures have also shown the need for stronger coordination, closer cooperation with Member States, and deeper engagement with international partners.
The EU Sanctions Office will be established within the Secretariat-General and will be under the political responsibility of Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque.
A central part of the new Office’s work will be to support the EU Sanctions Envoy, whose role is key to the EU’s efforts to prevent circumvention and work with partner countries. The Envoy engages with third countries to reduce the risk that EU sanctions are bypassed notably through alternative trade routes, financial channels, or procurement networks.
The Commission has appointed Lars DANIELSSON as International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions. Mr Danielsson will take up the position on 6 February 2027, when the mandate of the current Envoy, David O’SULLIVAN, ends. Mr Danielsson, a career Swedish diplomat with extensive diplomatic and EU experience, held senior positions in the Swedish Prime Minister’s Office, including as State Secretary for International and EU Affairs, and most recently served as Sweden’s Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the EU from 2016 to 2023.
As part of the creation of the new EU Sanctions Office, the Envoy will be attached to the Secretary-General and will keep a direct reporting line to Commissioner Albuquerque.
Next steps
These changes will take effect on 16 January 2027.
Background
The Office will support the EU Sanctions Envoy in the preparation, conduct and follow-up of missions, and will provide administrative and logistical support.
The new structure will bring together expertise from across the Commission, including from the Secretariat-General, DG FISMA, DG TRADE, DG TAXUD, OLAF and other relevant services. This will help ensure a more joined-up approach across the full sanctions cycle from policy design to implementation, enforcement, anti-circumvention and international outreach.
Quote(s)
EU sanctions are a central part of our response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. With each package we are eroding the foundations of Russia’s war economy. But to be effective, they must be fully implemented, rigorously enforced and protected against circumvention. And that is why we are creating the EU Sanctions Office, to strengthen our capacity and ensure the impact of all our sanctions regimes.
Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission
Sanctions are only as effective as our ability to implement and enforce them. The new EU Sanctions Office will strengthen coordination across the Commission, bringing together expertise from different policy areas to ensure a more coherent approach to sanctions, wherever and whenever they are needed. Working closely with Member States and international partners, we will reinforce implementation, close loopholes and prevent circumvention. A stronger, more coordinated European approach will make our sanctions more effective and our external action more credible.
Maria Luís Albuquerque, Commissioner for Financial Services and the Savings and Investments Union
Source – EU Commission
